subject: Probability and Stochastic Processes

projects.title: The Two Borel–Cantelli Lemmas
projects.idea: The summable case bounds the entire tail union. The independent divergent case instead bounds the probability that an entire long tail block contains no occurrence.
projects.target: For events AnA_n on a probability space, write {An i.o.}=⋂N≥1⋃n≥NAn\{A_n\text{ i.o.}\}=\bigcap_{N\ge1}\bigcup_{n\ge N}A_n. Prove: (i) if ∑nℙ(An)<∞\sum_n\mathbb P(A_n)<\infty, then ℙ(An i.o.)=0\mathbb P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0; (ii) if the events are mutually independent and ∑nℙ(An)=∞\sum_n\mathbb P(A_n)=\infty, then ℙ(An i.o.)=1\mathbb P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1. Mutual independence means every finite subcollection has product probability, including the corresponding complements.
imports: Use countable subadditivity, continuity of probability along monotone event sequences, finite-product independence, and 1−p≤e−p1-p\le e^{-p} for 0≤p≤10\le p\le1. These follow respectively from countable additivity and elementary real analysis. The first direction has no independence assumption.

nodes.title: Independent divergent tail control
nodes.role: Estimate the complementary event of no occurrence in a finite tail block and then exhaust the tail. Local obligation: Under independence and divergence, ℙ(An i.o.)=1\mathbb P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1.

projects.proof:
N1 — Summable tail control

  1. N1.1. Countable subadditivity gives ℙ(BN)≤∑n≥Nℙ(An)\mathbb P(B_N)\le\sum_{n\ge N}\mathbb P(A_n). The right side tends to zero because the series converges.

  2. N1.2. The events BNB_N decrease and their intersection is the infinitely-often event. Continuity from above yields its probability as lim⁡Nℙ(BN)=0\lim_N\mathbb P(B_N)=0.

N2 — Independent divergent tail control

  1. N2.1. Fix NN. For m≥Nm\ge N, independence gives ℙ(⋂n=NmAnc)=∏n=Nm(1−ℙ(An))≤exp⁡(−∑n=Nmℙ(An))\mathbb P(\bigcap_{n=N}^m A_n^c)=\prod_{n=N}^m(1-\mathbb P(A_n))\le\exp(-\sum_{n=N}^m\mathbb P(A_n)). Divergence makes this tend to zero as m→∞m\to\infty.

  2. N2.2. By continuity from above, ℙ(⋂n≥NAnc)=0\mathbb P(\bigcap_{n\ge N}A_n^c)=0, so ℙ(BN)=1\mathbb P(B_N)=1. The intersection of the countably many probability-one events BNB_N still has probability one, proving the second assertion.
projects.example: For independent fair coin tosses, let AnA_n be the event that toss nn is heads. The sum of probabilities diverges, so heads occur infinitely often almost surely. For a separate sequence of events BnB_n with ℙ(Bn)=2−n\mathbb P(B_n)=2^{-n}, the sum is finite, so only finitely many BnB_n occur almost surely regardless of their dependence.
boundary: Let An=AA_n=A for every nn, where ℙ(A)=1/2\mathbb P(A)=1/2. Then ∑nℙ(An)=∞\sum_n\mathbb P(A_n)=\infty, but the infinitely-often event is just AA, of probability 1/21/2. This disproves the divergent implication without a dependence hypothesis.

projects.title: Strong Law for IID Variables with a Finite Fourth Moment
projects.idea: The fourth moment supplies a summable n−2n^{-2} deviation bound. A countable collection of tolerances then upgrades eventual control to almost sure convergence.
projects.target: Let (Xn)n≥1(X_n)_{n\ge1} be independent identically distributed real random variables with 𝔼|X1|4<∞\mathbb E|X_1|^4<\infty and mean μ\mu. Prove n−1∑j=1nXj→μn^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n X_j\to\mu almost surely. This is the finite-fourth-moment version, not the optimal integrability form of the strong law.
imports: Import PS-01(i): summable event probabilities imply only finitely many occurrences almost surely. Use linearity of expectation, factorization of expectations of independent integrable products, and Markov’s inequality for nonnegative ZZ: ℙ(Z>a)≤𝔼Z/a\mathbb P(Z>a)\le\mathbb EZ/a for a>0a>0, obtained by Z≥a1{Z>a}Z\ge a1_{\{Z>a\}} and integration. Lower moments are finite by Hölder on a probability space. Centering preserves a finite fourth moment via |x−y|4≤8(|x|4+|y|4)|x-y|^4\le8(|x|^4+|y|^4).

projects.example: For IID Bernoulli(1/2)(1/2) variables, μ=1/2\mu=1/2, σ2=1/4\sigma^2=1/4, and m4=1/16m_4=1/16. Thus 𝔼Sn4=(3n2−2n)/16\mathbb ES_n^4=(3n^2-2n)/16, and ℙ(|n−1∑Xj−1/2|>ε)≤3/(16ε4n2)\mathbb P(|n^{-1}\sum X_j-1/2|>\varepsilon)\le3/(16\varepsilon^4n^2). Summability proves that the empirical proportion converges almost surely to 1/21/2.
boundary: If all variables are the same nonconstant Bernoulli variable ZZ, they are identically distributed with every moment finite, but their sample mean is always ZZ, not its mean 1/21/2. Independence is essential to this theorem. Conversely failure of a fourth moment does not itself refute a strong law; it only falls outside this proved version.

projects.title: Optional Stopping for Bounded Stopping Times
projects.idea: Stopping retains exactly those increments whose inclusion was decided before the next increment was observed. That predictability preserves their zero conditional means.
projects.target: Let (Mn,ℱn)n≥0(M_n,\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0} be an integrable real martingale: MnM_n is ℱn\mathcal F_n-measurable, 𝔼|Mn|<∞\mathbb E|M_n|<\infty, and 𝔼[Mn∣ℱn−1]=Mn−1\mathbb E[M_n\mid\mathcal F_{n-1}]=M_{n-1}. Let τ\tau be a stopping time with integer values and 0≤τ≤N0\le\tau\le N almost surely for some deterministic finite NN. Prove 𝔼Mτ=𝔼M0\mathbb EM_\tau=\mathbb EM_0. Also prove (Mn∧τ)(M_{n\wedge\tau}) is a martingale.
imports: Use linearity and the tower property of conditional expectation, and the pull-out property for bounded measurable factors. A stopping time means {τ≤n}∈ℱn\{\tau\le n\}\in\mathcal F_n. Finite sums of integrable variables are integrable. The boundedness condition is on the time, not on sample values of the martingale.

The stopped values are +1+1 with probability 1/21/2, 00 with probability 1/41/4, and −2-2 with probability 1/41/4. Their expectation is 1/2−1/2=0=M01/2-1/2=0=M_0, matching the theorem.

projects.title: Doob’s L2 Maximal Inequality
projects.idea: Partition the first crossing of a threshold by its time. Conditional expectation transfers that crossing value to the terminal absolute value; integrating thresholds produces the L2L^2 estimate.

imports: Use the tower and pull-out properties of conditional expectation, |𝔼[Z∣ℱ]|≤𝔼[|Z|∣ℱ]|\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F]|\le\mathbb E[|Z|\mid\mathcal F], Cauchy–Schwarz, and Tonelli for nonnegative integrands. The tail formula 𝔼Z2=∫0∞2λℙ(Z>λ)dλ\mathbb EZ^2=\int_0^\infty2\lambda\mathbb P(Z>\lambda)d\lambda follows by integrating Z2=∫0Z2λdλZ^2=\int_0^Z2\lambda d\lambda and applying Tonelli. projects.example: For a symmetric random walk with two increments and M0=0M_0=0, paths ++++ and −−-- have squared maximum four, while +−+- and −+-+ have squared maximum one. Thus 𝔼(Y*)2=(4+4+1+1)/4=5/2\mathbb E(Y^*)^2=(4+4+1+1)/4=5/2. The terminal second moment is two, and 5/2≤4⋅2=85/2\le4\cdot2=8. The bound controls the whole path, not merely its endpoint.
boundary: Adaptation alone is insufficient. The deterministic process M0=1,M1=0M_0=1,M_1=0 is adapted and square-integrable but not a martingale. Its maximal square is one while its terminal square is zero, contradicting the claimed inequality without the martingale hypothesis.

projects.title: Stationary Distribution and Mixing of a Positive Finite Markov Chain
projects.idea: Every row contains the same positive uniform component. Removing it leaves a stochastic remainder that cannot enlarge distance, so each step contracts by a common factor.
projects.target: Let P=(Pij)i,j=1dP=(P_{ij})_{i,j=1}^d be a row-stochastic matrix with every entry strictly positive. For row probability vectors, prove that there is a unique stationary distribution π\pi with πP=π\pi P=\pi, and ∥μPn−π∥1≤(1−δ)n∥μ−π∥1\|\mu P^n-\pi\|_1\le(1-\delta)^n\|\mu-\pi\|_1 for every initial distribution μ\mu and n≥0n\ge0, where ε=min⁡i,jPij\varepsilon=\min_{i,j}P_{ij} and δ=dε∈(0,1]\delta=d\varepsilon\in(0,1]. If δ=1\delta=1, convergence is exact after one step; the exponent-zero factor at n=0n=0 is interpreted as one.
imports: Use completeness of finite-dimensional Euclidean space, closedness of the probability simplex, the triangle inequality, and the geometric series. Total variation distance on this finite set is one half of the ℓ1\ell^1 distance. No spectral or Perron–Frobenius theorem is imported; the fixed point is constructed by a Cauchy estimate.

N2 — Construct the stationary limit

  1. N3.1. If π′\pi' is another stationary distribution, contraction gives ∥π−π′∥1≤q∥π−π′∥1\|\pi-\pi'\|_1\le q\|\pi-\pi'\|_1. Since q<1q<1, the norm is zero, proving uniqueness.

  2. N3.2. For any μ\mu, repeatedly compare μPn\mu P^n with πPn=π\pi P^n=\pi to obtain ∥μPn−π∥1≤qn∥μ−π∥1\|\mu P^n-\pi\|_1\le q^n\|\mu-\pi\|_1. When q=0q=0 the direct one-step conclusion applies. Thus existence, uniqueness, and the quantitative rate are all established.
projects.example: For P=(3/41/41/21/2)P=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/2&1/2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr), ε=1/4\varepsilon=1/4, δ=1/2\delta=1/2, and q=1/2q=1/2. Solving πP=π\pi P=\pi gives π=(2/3,1/3)\pi=(2/3,1/3). For μ=(1,0)\mu=(1,0), the initial ℓ1\ell^1 distance is 2/32/3; after one step it is |3/4−2/3|+|1/4−1/3|=1/6≤(1/2)(2/3)|3/4-2/3|+|1/4-1/3|=1/6\le(1/2)(2/3).
boundary: The nonnegative stochastic matrix (0110)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) has stationary distribution (1/2,1/2)(1/2,1/2) but alternates forever from (1,0)(1,0). Strict positivity is a sufficient mixing assumption here. It is not necessary for all mixing chains, but dropping it without a substitute invalidates this argument.
